      01

      Why we are here: everything on this page exists to make one guess better, the next word.

      Predict the next token

      Everything on this page serves one task: guess the next word. A language model does nothing else, so every mechanism added later has to pay for itself here. Switch between the two contexts in the first widget and watch the bars move. The last three words are identical in both sentences, so whatever the model does inside, it has to carry river or cheque all the way to the blank. The second widget shows the raw material it starts from: a token starts as a row of $d_{\text{model}}$ numbers, one per named coordinate (). One coordinate carries position. The names are illustrative, and the toy was written by hand so that the numbers agree with them. The sentence to remember: a good prediction needs a good representation of the relevant context.

      What could come next? Use all the words before the blank.

      The last three words are the same in both contexts.

      ↓ next-token probabilities

      A language model reads the tokens so far and assigns a probability to every possible next token: $$p(x_{t+1}\mid x_1,\ldots,x_t)$$

      To predict the next token well, the model needs a useful representation of everything relevant in the preceding context.

      The last three words, and watched the, are the same in both contexts, yet the answers differ. Whatever the model does inside, it must carry river or cheque forward to the blank. Where does it start?

      Choose a token. Its starting row is the sum below.

      Click a token in context A. Each column is one named coordinate (the names are illustrative; the numbers were chosen to agree with them); the last row is the sum of the two above it.

      A token embedding and a position vector have the same width:

      $$\ve{e_i^{(0)}} = \text{tok}_i + \text{pos}_i$$

      The result still has $d_{\text{model}}$ numbers. The superscript $(0)$ means before any contextual update.

      Every occurrence starts from its token's lookup row. Context will change the representation of this occurrence, not overwrite the lookup table.

      Keep in mind: the model is judged only by the probability it puts on the right next word, and the only thing it can work with is a row of numbers per token.

      02

      Why we are here: the crudest possible model, predicting from the last token alone, shows what "context" has to buy us.

      Baseline: only the last token

      This section is the crudest model on purpose. Only the last token reaches the output head, so the prediction is a function of one row of $d_{\text{model}}$ numbers. Switch the context in the widget and watch the bars: nothing moves. The table further down shows why, coordinate by coordinate. The word is the and the position is 10 in both sentences, so the starting representation is the same row of numbers, and the same row of numbers gives the same probabilities. The output head cannot tell a river scene from a bank branch, so it hedges across eight candidates. The sentence to remember: a prediction can only use what reaches it, and here almost nothing does.

      First try: let only the last known token reach the output head.

      Only the highlighted position is used.

      used: its $\ve{e_t}$ enters the output headnot used: invisible to the prediction

      →

      output headthen softmax

      Context:

      Same last token + same position → same input row → same prediction.

      The starting row $\ve{e_t^{(0)}}$ goes straight to the output head:

      $$\ell = \ve{e_t^{(0)}}\,W_{\text{vocab}} + b$$
      $$p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\ell)$$

      We sometimes write the current row simply as $\ve{e_t}$. At this stage it is still $\ve{e_t^{(0)}}$; no contextual update has happened. $$\ell = \ve{e_t}\,W_{\text{vocab}} + b, \qquad p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\ell)$$

      If context is to matter, its information must reach the row before the head reads it.

      The distribution is almost flat: eight candidates, all near the same height. The model cannot prefer water to teller because, from its point of view, the two sentences are the same sentence. The table shows that sentence, coordinate by coordinate.

      The only input, in both contexts

      Keep in mind: the output head sees one row of numbers. If the context is to matter, the context has to be written into that row before it arrives.

      03

      Why we are here: the obvious fix, handing the model the last w tokens, and why it is not enough.

      Baseline: a fixed window of w tokens

      The natural fix is to hand the model more tokens: concatenate the last $w$ representations into one long row and let a bigger matrix read it. The first widget sketches that as a network: the input column is the window, and the first layer's input width grows with the window. Drag the second slider and watch which tokens sit inside the window and how the input grows by five numbers per token. Set $w$ to 3 and river falls outside. Set it to 10 and every token is in, but only because this sentence is short. The included embeddings still carry content: a network can learn to treat river differently from the. The limitation is the fixed input width and hard boundary, not an inability to use the words. The sentence to remember: a window decides by position what to include, and we want to decide by content.

      Why not simply hand the model the last $w$ tokens? Their rows feed a fixed network: a first layer that reads all $w$ rows at once, a hidden layer, and one output per vocabulary word.

      More input tokens → a wider first layer

      Sketch, not the toy's arithmetic: the hidden width $h$ is a stated choice, the outputs are the toy vocabulary with the answer for context A marked. Drag the slider or press the arrow key.

      The window size is baked into the shape of the first layer before any word is read. The hidden width and output matrix can stay unchanged; it is the input-to-hidden matrix that grows.

      Concatenate the previous $w$ token representations into one long vector and predict from that. $w$ denotes the window width; we reserve $K$ for the matrix of attention keys later.

      Choose the window: which tokens reach the prediction?

      A word behind the boundary is unavailable, not merely down-weighted.

      $$c_t = [\ve{e_{t-w+1}};\,\ldots;\,\ve{e_t}] \in \mathbb R^{w d_{\text{model}}}$$
      $$p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t}) = \operatorname{softmax}(c_t W + b)$$
      $W$ has shape $w d_{\text{model}}\times |\mathcal V|$.

      Anything before the previous $w$ tokens is absent.

      A longer sentence can always put a useful clue beyond that boundary.

      Each input slot is set by its distance from the end.

      The network can respond to the words in those slots. What stays fixed is how many slots there are and which positions are supplied.

      There is no explicit query-dependent retrieval step in this baseline. This does not mean that an MLP is incapable of using content within a sufficiently large window.

      Two prediction positions in the same sentence

      The outlined words are illustrative: they are computed from the largest weights of the later toy mechanism. A sufficiently large window includes both sets, but still retains one hard boundary.

      Could we collect useful information without growing the input width every time the prefix grows?

      Keep in mind: a fixed window chooses tokens by where they are, never by what they say. The rest of the page builds a mechanism that chooses by content.

      04

      Why we are here: a fixed window imposes a hard boundary on which earlier tokens are available. Could we instead pool information from the whole prefix?

      Weighted pooling: where should weights come from?

      Attention is a way to choose weights, so this section first shows what weights do. A pooled vector $c_i$ is a weighted sum of earlier representations, and the spreadsheets below make that sum visible: one row per token, one column per coordinate, a weight column on the left and the sum in the footer. Drag the position slider and watch the mean give every included row the same weight. Then move the raw-weight sliders for bank and watch the footer drift towards whichever row you favour. The sentence to remember: the weights decide what a token collects, and someone has to choose them.

      Drop the window: combine every available input row into one fixed-width row.

      $$c_i = \frac{1}{i}\sum_{j \le i} \ve{e_j}$$

      Choose how much of the prefix is available.

      For bank, river may carry more useful information than the.

      $$c_i = \sum_{j \le i} \va{\alpha_{ij}}\, \ve{e_j}, \qquad \sum_{j} \va{\alpha_{ij}} = 1$$

      The weight $\va{\alpha_{ij}}$ says how much position $i$ takes from source $j$.

      The raw weights are normalized to sum to 1.

      You chose those weights by hand, because you know that bank wants river. A model cannot ask you, and a different token would want a different set of weights.

      Where should the weights $\va{\alpha_{ij}}$ come from?

      They should depend on what token $i$ currently needs and what information token $j$ contains. Both are functions of the representations themselves, $\ve{e_i}$ and $\ve{e_j}$. Attention is a way to build that function.

      Keep in mind: the pooled vector is only as good as its weights, and the weights we want depend on the token that is asking and on the tokens that could answer. The next section hands that job to a search engine.

      05

      Why we are here: weights should come from what a token needs and what a token has. Search gives us a familiar analogy for those two roles.

      A detour through search: Query, Key, Value

      Before attention touches a sentence, it helps to see the same three roles somewhere familiar. A video site has to answer two questions for every item: does it match the search, and what should it hand back? Those are different jobs, so each video keeps a key for matching and a value for returning. The first spreadsheet puts the query in the top row and the six keys beneath it, so you can compare them column by column; the score on the right is the dot product. Switch to the overfitting question and watch which row wins. The sentence to remember: keys decide whether to retrieve, values are what gets retrieved.

      A user asks a video site a question. That request is the query.

      What are we looking for?

      Two separate jobs: decide which items match, then decide what information to return.

      Six results, ranked by key scoreOpen a result to see its key calculation and value.
      Query

      The query describes the request. Each item's key describes when it is a useful match.

      Multiply matching coordinates, then add: $s_j=\vq{q}\cdot\vk{k_j}$.

      Matching is a dot product between the query and each key. At this stage the site looks at nothing else about the item.

      $$s_j = \vq{q}\cdot \vk{k_j}$$

      $\vq{q}$ = query representation, $\vk{k_j}$ = key of item $j$, $\vv{v_j}$ = value of item $j$.

      QWhat am I looking for?the query, formed by the searcher
      KWhen should you retrieve me?the key, one per item, used for matching
      VWhat information do I send?the value, one per item, the payload

      The Value of each video: what comes back if it is retrieved

      The key chose the item. The value supplies the information returned.

      A high score says retrieve Backpropagation, but what arrives is its value, not its key. For this toy lookup, take the highest-scoring item. Real search engines usually rank several results; attention instead mixes values using soft weights.

      Keep in mind: a score comes from the query and the key alone. The value plays no part in matching; it only travels once its item is chosen.

      06

      Why we are here: hard retrieval chooses the single best match. Attention returns a mixture. We go back to the gradient question (query 1) with the same keys and values as before.

      Hard retrieval → soft retrieval

      Our hard-retrieval baseline picks the best-scoring item and returns its value. Attention instead blends values according to how well each key matched the query. This section makes that blend a spreadsheet: the scores from the previous section feed a softmax, the weights fill the $\va{\alpha_j}$ column, every value row is scaled by its weight, and the footer adds the rows up. Start in hard mode, where one row carries all the weight, then switch to soft and lower the temperature to watch the two modes meet. Drag a score up and watch every weight move. The sentence to remember: attention returns a weighted mixture of values, not one value.

      In our hard-retrieval baseline, choose the key with the largest score and return that item's value:

      $$j^* = \arg\max_j\, \vq{q}\cdot \vk{k_j}, \qquad \text{return } \vv{v_{j^*}}$$
      If two items are useful, why return information from only one?

      The scores from the gradient-information query

      First exponentiate each score: $s_j\mapsto e^{s_j}$.

      Then divide each result by the same total:

      $$\va{\alpha_j}=\frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_r e^{s_r}}$$
      These weights are shares over input items, not probabilities of the next word.

      Attention returns a weighted mixture of information for the current query—not another set of match scores.

      A score changed by a slider no longer equals the original dot product. Treat it as a controlled intervention on the matching result, as if the key had changed.

      In soft mode the weights are $\va{\alpha_j} = \operatorname{softmax}_j(s_j/\tau)$. A small $\tau$ makes the mixture sharper. As $\tau \to 0$, soft retrieval becomes hard retrieval when one score is strictly the largest; tied top scores keep sharing the weight. $\tau = 1$ is the formula above.

      $\va{\alpha}=\operatorname{softmax}(s/\tau)$: smaller $\tau$ → sharper weights.

      Each piece now has a job. A Query says what the searcher needs, Keys decide who matches, Values carry what comes back, and softmax turns scores into a mixture. Back to language.

      Keep in mind: the scores decide the weights, the weights decide the mixture, and a change in one score moves every weight at once, because the softmax keeps them summing to 1.

      07

      Why we are here: search results carried a key and a value. Now every token in the sentence gets its own.

      Every token becomes a searchable record

      The search detour gave us three roles: a query that asks, a key that says when to answer, and a value that is the answer. Now every token gets a key and a value, computed from its own representation with two shared matrices, and the token gathering context gets a query from a third matrix.

      Every coordinate has a name in this toy, so read the column headers before the numbers. Click a different query token and watch which rows stay open. Open a record and read its three rows. The sentence to remember: a query, a key and a value are three linear views of the same $\ve{e}$.

      Bank is the receiver. It needs information from the words it has read.

      Its query describes what to look for: $\vq{q_i}=\ve{e_i}W_Q$.

      Each source publishes a key to match against: $\vk{k_j}=\ve{e_j}W_K$.

      The same source publishes a value to send: $\vv{v_j}=\ve{e_j}W_V$.

      The query and key choose where to read. The value supplies what is read.

      Vectors are rows throughout this page. A representation has $d_{\text{model}}$ numbers; multiplying by a $d_{\text{model}}\times d_k$ projection produces $d_k$ numbers. Queries and keys share matching axes because a dot product compares corresponding coordinates. Values have their own axes, and may have a different width, because they are mixed rather than compared. The named coordinates are illustrative; the arithmetic is real.

      A value is made from the embedding; it is not necessarily the embedding itself.

      Values: what each open record sends if it is read

      q_i = e_i @ W_Q
k_j, v_j = e_j @ W_K, e_j @ W_V

      Keep in mind: nothing has been compared or retrieved yet. Each token has only been given a query, a key and a value, all computed from its own $\ve{e}$ with matrices that every position shares.

      08

      Why we are here: one query, seven records. Attention happens in two separate phases: deciding where to read, then reading.

      Two jobs: choose weights, then mix values

      Attention is easier to trust once you see that it is two separate jobs. Phase A uses only queries and keys: it scores every earlier token and turns the scores into weights that sum to one. Phase B uses only values: each token sends its value, scaled by its weight, and the scaled values are added.

      Run phase A, then click a key in the picture to see its dot product written out, axis by axis. Then run phase B and read the sum, one coordinate per line.       Phase B: use those weights to mix the seven $\vv{v_j}$ rows.

      09

      Why we are here: the retrieved message $m_i$ must get back into the token’s representation. This is the centre of the whole story.

      The contextual update Δe

      This is the step the whole page builds towards. The message $m_7$ is a mixture of values, so it lives in value space with $d_v$ coordinates. $W_O$ maps it into the $d_{\text{model}}$ coordinates of a representation, and that vector, $\vd{\Delta e_7}$, is added to $\ve{e_7}$. The residual branch keeps the original row as an input to the addition; the resulting row combines it with context.

      Press Play, or step through, and watch the highlight move down the diagram. The following block writes out its numerical result; hover a cell of the final row to see the addition. Read the axis names: the message speaks in value coordinates, $W_O$ turns them into representation coordinates. The sentence to remember: attention computes the update; the residual connection adds it to the representation we started from.

      The message $m_i$ lives in value space ($d_v$ numbers). An output projection $W_O$ maps it into representation space ($d_{\text{model}}$ numbers). We call that vector the contextual update $\vd{\Delta e_i}$ and add it to $\ve{e_i}$.

      $$m_i = \sum_{j \le i} \va{\alpha_{ij}}\, \vv{v_j} \qquad \boxed{\vd{\Delta e_i} = m_i\,W_O} \qquad \boxed{\vp{e_i^{\text{new}}} = \ve{e_i} + \vd{\Delta e_i}}$$

      The attention branch computes an update; the residual branch preserves $\ve{e_7}$

      Two inputs meet at $+$: the old row $\ve{e_7}$ and the context-dependent update $\vd{\Delta e_7}$.

      The numerical result of the eight-step path

      Message → representation-space update → residual addition

      The output projection: $m_7$ (value space, $1 \times d_v$) $\to$ $\vd{\Delta e_7}$ (representation space, $1 \times d_{\text{model}}$)

      Attention computes context-dependent information. The residual connection adds that update to the existing representation.
      Calling this update $\vd{\Delta e_i}$ is pedagogical notation used on this page; it is not standard Transformer notation. Standard implementations usually call it the attention output and add it through a residual connection. The addition itself is standard: it is the residual connection around the attention sublayer.

      PyTorch · $m_i$ is $1 \times d_v$; $\Delta e_i$ and $e_i$ are $1 \times d_{\text{model}}$.

      delta_e_i = m_i @ W_O
e_new_i = e_i + delta_e_i

      Keep in mind: $\vp{e_7'} = \ve{e_7} + \vd{\Delta e_7}$. The right branch computed the update, the left branch carried $\ve{e_7}$ unchanged, and the plus joins them. That plus is the residual connection.

      11

      Why we are here: a common confusion. Are queries, keys and values new lookup tables or the updated token row? Neither: they are projections used during attention.

      What exactly are Q, K, and V?

      Queries, keys and values are three projected views of the current representation, not three independently learned lookup tables. Pick any token in the chips and read the four rows: the three lower rows are computed from the single $\ve{e}$ row above them by three fixed matrices, and nothing else about the token changes. The axis names say what each row means: a query row is what the token asks for, a key row is what it offers, a value row is what it sends. Below them sit the three matrices themselves, shared by every token. Step through the lifetime strip to see when each row exists inside one attention layer. The sentence to remember: $\vq{q}$, $\vk{k}$ and $\vv{v}$ are working vectors made from $\ve{e}$, and $\ve{e} + \vd{\Delta e}$ is the updated token row passed to the next sublayer.

      Take the current representation of one token, $\ve{e_i}$. Three fixed matrices read it and produce three short rows. They are working vectors computed from $\ve{e_i}$; none of them replaces it.

      $$\ve{e_i} \;\rightarrow\; \begin{cases} \vq{q_i} = \ve{e_i}\,W_Q \\[2pt] \vk{k_i} = \ve{e_i}\,W_K \\[2pt] \vv{v_i} = \ve{e_i}\,W_V \end{cases}$$

      Pick a token. The top row is the only input. Each lower row is that row times its shared projection: $W_Q,W_K$ produce $d_k$ matching coordinates; $W_V$ produces $d_v$ value coordinates. Read the axis names above the cells.

      q and k share the same three columns because the dot product compares them column by column. v has its own two columns, and its own width, because it is only mixed and sent.

      The three matrices, shared by every token

      Lifetime inside one attention layer

      Step through the layer and watch which rows exist at each moment: $\ve{e_i}$ persists, $\vq{q_i}, \vk{k_i}, \vv{v_i}$ are computed and used, $\vd{\Delta e_i}$ is added to $\ve{e_i}$.

      The strip scrolls sideways on narrow screens; the lit column follows the stepper.

      The one chain, again

      The three projections sit in the second box; they are inputs to attention, and only $\vd{\Delta e}$ comes out of it.

      Keep in mind: the token representation is $\ve{e}$, before and after. $\vq{q}$, $\vk{k}$ and $\vv{v}$ were made from it and used, and $\vd{\Delta e}$ is what came back.

      12

      Why we are here: a small technical fix. The spread of raw dot products grows with the dimension, and dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ takes that growth out.

      Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?

      Softmax is sensitive to score differences. Under the independence assumptions below, the typical spread of a dot product grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$; not every individual dot product must grow. The first illustration holds four raw scores fixed and changes only the divisor. It shows what scaling does, not how score variance grows. A separate seeded simulation checks the variance argument, and the final table returns to our actual bank query.

      The score between a query and a key is a dot product over $d_k$ coordinates. Standard attention divides it by $\sqrt{d_k}$:

      $$s_{ij} = \frac{\vq{q_i}\cdot\vk{k_j}}{\sqrt{d_k}}$$

      For intuition, assume all query and key coordinates are mutually independent, mean 0, variance 1. Then $\operatorname{Var}(q_l k_l)=1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\vq{q}\cdot\vk{k})=d_k$. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{d_k}$.

      Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ makes the variance 1 under those assumptions. Learned coordinates need not obey them exactly: this is a scale-control argument, not a promise that attention is always diffuse.

      scores = (Q @ K.T) / math.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])

      Four fixed raw scores, with and without scaling illustrative numbers

      Hold the raw scores $r=[0,0.5,1.5,-0.5]$ fixed. The scaled scores are $s=r/\sqrt{d_k}$. Increasing the divisor flattens softmax(scaled), while softmax(raw) stays fixed.

      Why the dot product grows with $d_k$: a seeded simulation

      Read down the first column: the variance of the raw dot product tracks $d_k$. The second column stays near 1.

      In the toy model (dk = ): bank reading the first 7 tokens

      Same four columns, real numbers. The note in the following block says how much the factor $\sqrt{d_k}$ changes the top weight.

      Scaling preserves the score ranking. It controls how strongly softmax concentrates on the highest scores.
      scores = (q_bank @ K.T) / math.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
alpha = scores.softmax(dim=-1)

      Keep in mind: scaling counteracts the expected growth due to dimension. Learned vector lengths and alignment still affect score differences, so attention can remain sharp.

      13

      Why we are here: this is next-token prediction, so a token may read the past and never the future.

      Causal masking

      The model is trained to predict the next token, so during training the answer for position $i$ sits right there at position $i+1$. This section shows what stops a token from reading it. Switch the causal mask off and watch row 5: with the mask on, token 5 (the) reads only tokens 1 to 5; with it off, much of its weight lands on future tokens: river is its immediate target, and bank is additional future information. Press the send button in both states and compare the message that arrives. The sentence to remember: token $i$ may read from $j \le i$ and never from $j > i$, and the mask enforces that with a $-\infty$ before the softmax.

      At position $i$, the model must predict token $i+1$.

      At generation time, token $i+1$ does not exist yet.

      Therefore the query at $i$ may read only keys at $j\le i$.

      If position $i$ could read position $i+1$ during training, it could read the answer it is being graded on.

      Every position predicts its next token at the same time

      Training does not run one query at a time. One pass through the sentence scores every position at once: each token is a query, reads the tokens up to itself, and is graded on the token that follows it.

      Short sequence shown; the ten-token sentence continues the same staircase. Position $i$ may read tokens $1 \ldots i$ and must predict token $i+1$.

      The rule, written twice illustrative 4×4

      Same rule on both sides: the picture on the left, the mask matrix $M$ that section 16 will use on the right.

      Allowed and masked

      $$\begin{bmatrix} \checkmark & \times & \times & \times\\ \checkmark & \checkmark & \times & \times\\ \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \times\\ \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark \end{bmatrix}$$

      Row $i$ = query token, column $j$ = key token. $\checkmark$: allowed ($j \le i$). $\times$: masked ($j > i$).

      As a mask matrix

      Adding $-\infty$ before the softmax is the same as deleting that column for that row: $e^{-\infty} = 0$.

      Start with every query-key score:

      $$S=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$$

      Add $M_{ij}=-\infty$ wherever $j>i$.

      Then $e^{-\infty}=0$, so those attention weights are exactly zero.

      scores = scores.masked_fill(future, float('-inf'))
weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)

      The real attention matrix $\va{A}$ for sentence A (10 tokens), with the mask on or off

      Toggle the mask and watch the hatched triangle: with the mask off, weight moves into it, and the outlined cells $(i, i+1)$ are where each token could read its own answer. Click any cell for the score arithmetic behind its weight.

      Hover a cell to read one weight.

      One leak, up close: token 5 (“the”) whose next token is “river”

      Compare the two rows: the mask-off row can read its immediate target, river, and other future tokens such as bank. Press the button to see which tokens send.

      The loss asks for $p(x_{i+1}\mid x_{\le i})$.

      Without the mask, the representation at $i$ can contain $x_{i+1}$ itself.

      That shortcut disappears at generation time, exactly when the model must work.

      Token $i$ may retrieve from $j\le i$, never from $j>i$.

      Keep in mind: with the mask off the rows still sum to 1, so the leak is invisible in the totals and visible only in where the weight went. The mask is not a detail of one example; it is what makes next-token training honest.

      14

      Why we are here: a contextual representation is only useful if it changes the prediction.

      From Δe to the next-token probabilities

      Sections 09 to 13 built an updated vector for bank. Now extend the prefix through “and watched the” and predict the token after that final the. Its query, not bank’s query, determines this attention row. In this single-layer toy, earlier words reach the prediction through the update to that last position. Switch the context between the river and cheque sentences: the attention row, update and probabilities change. Then bypass attention and switch again: the probability row stays fixed, just as in section 02.

      The known prefix now has ten tokens. The final the supplies $\vq{q_{10}}$; we predict what follows it. Bank’s earlier query $\vq{q_7}$ is not reused.

      Earlier: bank at position 7 received context through $\vq{q_7}$.

      Now: the at position 10 receives context through $\vq{q_{10}}$.

      The next token is still unknown. It cannot supply the query.

      q_last = E[-1] @ W_Q  # the current last known position

      Where the last token reads from

      Context
      1 · Match

      $r_j=q_{10}\cdot k_j$

      2 · Scale

      $s_{10,j}=r_j/\sqrt{d_k}$

      3 · Normalize

      $\alpha_{10,j}=\operatorname{softmax}(s_{10,:})_j$

      scores = (q_last @ K.T) / math.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
alpha = scores.softmax(dim=-1)  # ten source weights; sum = 1

      The update, added axis by axis

      Mix

      $m_{10}=\alpha_{10,:}V$

      $1\times d_v$

      Project

      $\Delta e_{10}=m_{10}W_O$

      $1\times d_{\rm model}$

      Add

      $e'_{10}=e_{10}+\Delta e_{10}$

      $1\times d_{\rm model}$

      delta_last = (alpha @ V) @ W_O
e_last_new = E[-1] + delta_last

      The output head: logits, then probabilities

      $$\ell = \vp{e_{10}'}\,W_{\text{vocab}} + b, \qquad p(x_{11}\mid x_{\le10}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\ell)$$
      Attention softmax

      One weight per known source position.

      Vocabulary softmax

      One probability per possible next token.

      logits = e_last_new @ W_vocab + b_vocab
p_next = logits.softmax(dim=-1)

      The denominator includes every token in the vocabulary, not only the few candidates shown in the table.

      The causal chain

      Watch the boxes light up in order when you change the context. Earlier tokens reach the head only through the update they send to the last token.

      Forward computation changes the token states for this input. It does not change the stored projection matrices or embedding table.

      This layer

      $\ve{e_7}\rightarrow\vv{v_7}$

      The final the can read bank’s input-derived value.

      The next layer

      $\vp{e_7'}\rightarrow$ new key and value

      The updated bank representation becomes a new layer input.

      Parallel updates do not read one another’s newly updated rows.

      Keep in mind: the head never sees the earlier tokens. It sees one row, $\vp{e_t'} = \ve{e_t} + \vd{\Delta e_t}$, and everything the context contributes is inside $\vd{\Delta e_t}$.

      16

      Why we are here: one token at a time is clear. Now every token does the same thing at once, and that is what the matrices say.

      The same thing in matrix form

      Section 15 followed one token, bank, through attention. Every other token runs the same arithmetic on its own row, and nothing in that arithmetic depends on which row you look at. That is why the whole sublayer fits in a handful of matrix products: each product does the section 15 step for all seven tokens at once.

      Step through the operations below and keep your eye on row 7. At every stage it holds the numbers you already saw for bank. The sentence to remember: a row of the matrix is a token, and $\vp{E'} = \ve{E} + \vd{\Delta E}$ updates every row in one addition.

      Stack the current row representations of the short seven-token prefix as one matrix. Every row of $\ve{E}$ is one $\ve{e_i}$; every operation from section 15 now happens for all $T$ rows in a single product.

      $$\ve{E} = \begin{bmatrix} \ve{e_1} \\ \vdots \\ \ve{e_T} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \vq{Q} = \ve{E}\,W_Q, \quad \vk{K} = \ve{E}\,W_K, \quad \vv{V} = \ve{E}\,W_V$$

      Dimensions, always in view

      Every matrix with $T$ rows has one row per token; row 7 is bank in all of them.

      One matrix operation at a time

      Row labels are tokens, column labels are the named coordinates. The outlined row is bank, the section 15 computation. Click any score cell for its arithmetic.

      $S = \dfrac{\vq{Q}\,\vk{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ $\va{A} = \operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S + M)$
      Routing result: row $i$ of $\va{A}$ contains the source weights chosen by receiver $i$.

      Use the weights, then preserve the input

      $H = \va{A}\,\vv{V}$ $\vd{\Delta E} = H\,W_O$ $\boxed{\vp{E'} = \ve{E} + \vd{\Delta E}}$

      Each row of $H$ is one receiver’s weighted mixture. $W_O$ returns it to model width before the residual addition.

      PyTorch · matrices are row-major; mask contains 0 or −∞.

      A = (Q @ K.T / d_k**0.5 + mask).softmax(dim=-1)
E_new = E + (A @ V) @ W_O

      Keep in mind: the matrices are bookkeeping, not a new idea. Row $i$ of $\vp{E'}$ is $\ve{e_i} + \vd{\Delta e_i}$, the softmax runs one row at a time, and the mask is what keeps row $i$ from reading columns $j > i$.

      17

      Why we are here: the fixed window (03) and mean pooling (04) return, with one more fixed scheme, to be lined up against attention.

      Attention versus the alternatives

      Sections 03 and 04 set aside the fixed window and the plain mean because their inclusion or pooling rule is fixed, although their outputs still depend on the input words. This section puts those two schemes, a distance-decay scheme and attention into one table, so the difference shows up in the numbers instead of in an argument.

      Switch between the river sentence and the cheque sentence and watch the rows. The first three rows do not change at all: their weights were fixed before any word was read. Only the attention row moves, and it moves toward the words that matter for the blank. The sentence to remember: attention is the only scheme whose weights are computed from the content.

      All four schemes use input information for the last token $t = 10$ from $\ve{e_1},\ldots,\ve{e_t}$. One question separates them: who sets the weights, and do they read the words? Switch the sentence and watch which row reacts.

      Choose the context

      Four weighting schemes, one table

      Look at the last row: its weights favour different evidence, and only that weight row changes when you switch the sentence.

      What each scheme does with the context

      SchemeContext for the last tokenWho sets the weightsWhat is retrieved
      Fixed window$c_t = [\ve{e_{t-w+1}};\,\ldots;\,\ve{e_t}]$Position determines inclusion; the network can still use the content of each included embedding$\ve{e_j}$, concatenated
      Mean pooling$c_t = \frac{1}{t}\sum_{j \le t} \ve{e_j}$Nobody. Every token gets $1/t$$\ve{e_j}$, averaged

      Read the third column: three schemes fix inclusion or pooling weights; attention recomputes its mixing weights from the content.

      Two weighted sums, two very different rules

      SchemeContext for the last tokenWho sets the weightsWhat is retrieved
      Fixed positional weights$c_t = \sum_{j \le t} w_j\, \ve{e_j}$Distance. Same distance means the same weight$\ve{e_j}$, weighted
      Attention$m_t = \sum_{j \le t} \va{\alpha_{tj}}\vv{v_j}$Content. $\va{\alpha_{tj}}$ comes from $\vq{q_t}\cdot \vk{k_j}$$\vv{v_j}$, then $\vd{\Delta e_t}=m_tW_O$

      Keep in mind: a window, a mean and a distance decay all fix their weights before reading the sentence. Attention computes $\va{\alpha_{ij}}$ from $\vq{q_i}$ and $\vk{k_j}$, so the same position can receive very different mixing weights in different sentences.

      Pause and think

      By now you have seen every object on the page at least twice. This section exists because the confusions that survive a lecture are always the same ones: mixing up keys and values, taking the query for the new representation, or treating $\vd{\Delta e}$ as standard notation.

The sentence to remember: queries, keys and values are working vectors; the token row passed onward is $\vp{e_i'} = \ve{e_i} + \vd{\Delta e_i}$.

      Notation recap, one token at a time

      Match: $\vq{q_i},\vk{k_j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k}$.
      Compatible coordinates for comparing a request and a source.
      Send: $\vv{v_j},\vm{m_i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$.
      Values and their weighted mixture share the message space.
      Update: $\ve{e_i},\vd{\Delta e_i},\vp{e_i'}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$.
      The input and its update must have the same width to add.

      Check the shape column: only $\ve{e_i}$, $\vd{\Delta e_i}$ and $\vp{e_i'}$ live in the model space of width $d_{\text{model}}$.

      Keep in mind: $\vk{k_j}$ decides whether token $j$ is read and $\vv{v_j}$ decides what it sends; $\vq{q_i}$ is a matching projection, not the updated token row; the update is added through the residual connection $\vp{e_i'} = \ve{e_i} + \vd{\Delta e_i}$.

      Why we are here: the whole argument three times (in words, as a chain, and as matrices), then back to the first sentence.

      Three summaries

      A summary is only useful if you can reproduce it without the page. So this section says the same thing three times, each in a form you might be asked for: a sentence for a conversation, a chain for a whiteboard, and four equations for an exam.

      Play the chain and watch the pipeline diagram light up stage by stage. Then switch the sentence in the last card and check that the winning word changes while the equations do not. The sentence to remember: each token reads itself and earlier tokens, mixes their values, and receives the projected message through a residual addition.

      1 · Intuitive

      Each token matches its query against its own and earlier keys, mixes the corresponding values, and receives a context-dependent update through a residual addition.

      2 · Operational

      Watch the box and the pipeline stage light up together: the chain and the diagram are the same six steps.

      3 · Mathematical

      $M$ is the causal mask ($-\infty$ above the diagonal, $0$ elsewhere);

      Read the shapes on the right: only the boxed line returns to $T \times d_{\text{model}}$, the space every token started in.

      3 · Mathematical, continued

      Routing chooses where to read; this phase determines what information changes each row.

      From $\vp{E'}$ to the next token

      Switch the sentence: the last token is “the” in both. Its updated row carries the context to the vocabulary head.

      PyTorch · one vocabulary distribution from the final updated row.

      logits = E_new[-1] @ W_vocab + b
probs = logits.softmax(dim=-1)

      1 · PredictThe final known position supplies its query. The head returns $p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t})$.
      2 · ChooseFor a greedy step, select the highest-probability candidate.
      3 · AppendThe chosen token becomes position $t+1$ in the known prefix.
      4 · RepeatForm the new final query $q_{t+1}=e_{t+1}W_Q$ and predict $x_{t+2}$.
      next_id = probs.argmax().reshape(1)  # greedy decoding
tokens = torch.cat([tokens, next_id])  # same parameters; a longer prefix
      Forward

      Prefix $\rightarrow$ prediction $p$

      Use the same attention and vocabulary head we just traced.

      Measure error

      $L=-\log p(y)$

      $y$ is the observed next token in the training text.

      Learn

      Autograd computes gradients; the optimizer updates the embedding table and weight matrices.

      optimizer.zero_grad(); loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, target)
loss.backward(); optimizer.step()

      What this example has, and what it does not yet have

      • One attention head computes a contextual update; residual addition forms $e_i' = e_i + \Delta e_i$.
      • The vocabulary head reads the final updated row to give next-token probabilities.
      • Generation repeats that prediction with a growing prefix and fixed parameters.
      • Training updates parameters; stacked layers apply further transformations. Those are different operations.

      Every symbol on this page in one place; the shape column uses the toy sizes.

      Part 3 adds several heads, stacked layers and the rest of the Transformer.

      Keep in mind: attention computes $\vd{\Delta E}$ and the residual connection forms $\vp{E'} = \ve{E} + \vd{\Delta E}$; and the output head reads the last row of $\vp{E'}$ to predict the next token.
